explanations: terra: Israel's rescue from Pharaoh's slaughter is called a great بلاء from their Lord; deliverance and severe harm occupy one divinely governed ordeal.

luna: Israel’s covenant includes doing good to orphans; it makes care for them a standing communal duty, alongside family and the poor. | terra: The covenant commands good treatment of parents, kin, orphans, and the poor; honoring the orphan belongs to a foundational social obligation.
terra: Abraham is tested with commands and fulfills them before being made a leader, so rank follows faithful response to trial rather than material reception.
terra: God says even the unbeliever will receive temporary provision before judgment, proving that worldly supply cannot by itself mean divine honor.

luna: The command to compete in good works gives a Quranic form to the section’s dictionary definition of ك ر م as outdoing another in generosity, turning competition toward deeds. | terra: فاستبقوا الخيرات commands people to outstrip one another in good deeds, a general Quranic form of the section's generosity-race dictionary sense.

luna: The ayah uses the section’s root ب ل و for testing and names loss of wealth among its trials; it gives a specific form of constriction that the section says should not be read as humiliation. | terra: Fear, hunger, and loss of wealth, lives, and crops are named as tests; it expands the harmful side of the section's two-sided ibtilā into concrete forms.

luna: The ayah makes spending beloved wealth on orphans part of righteousness; this joins the section’s definition of ك ر م as generosity with the orphan who needs it. | terra: Birr includes giving loved wealth to orphans and other dependents, so true righteousness and honor are measured by transferred benefit rather than possession.
terra: Worldly life is beautified for disbelievers who mock believers, yet the people of taqwa are above them at resurrection and God provides without account.

luna: Asked what to spend, the ayah lists orphans among those to whom resources go; it makes the section’s care an allocation of provision, not a self-description. | terra: When asked what to spend, the answer expressly includes parents, kin, orphans, poor, and traveler; the cared-for person is turned toward a widening circle of care.

luna: Asked about orphans, the ayah says setting their affairs right is best and calls them brothers; it directly answers the section’s account of the orphan’s care being neglected or delayed. | terra: Concerning orphans, إصلاح لهم is best and living together is framed as brotherhood; the verse replaces neglect with accountable household inclusion.

luna: The ayah details nursing a child, the father’s duty to provide and clothe, and the parents’ shared decision about weaning; it makes the section’s image of a child raised and sustained through care concrete. | terra: Nursing, the father's duty of food and clothing, consultation, and protection from parental harm spell out the material work hidden inside the section's image of a child raised in care.
terra: The call to lend God a good loan is paired with God contracting and expanding; generosity is required under the same sovereign variation the section describes.
terra: Those who spend must not follow their gift with reminders or injury; received help may not be turned into the kind of status debt Pharaoh asserts over Moses.
terra: Kind speech and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury; material giving without honoring the recipient fails the section's outward meaning of ikram.
terra: Charity is nullified by reminders, injury, display, and lack of faith, distinguishing genuine ikram from a giver's performance of superiority.
terra: Givers must spend from good things they earned and not choose inferior goods they themselves would accept only reluctantly; the recipient must be treated with honor.
terra: Satan promises poverty while God promises forgiveness and bounty; anticipated restriction is identified as the pressure that can choke generosity.
terra: Self-restrained poor people can be mistaken for rich and remain unrecognized; it specifies how need is overlooked and goodness reaches the dependent late.
terra: Children, accumulated gold and silver, livestock, and cultivated land are listed as beautified desires and then called only the provision of worldly life.
terra: The next ayah offers enduring gardens and God's approval as better than the status objects of 3:14, separating true favor from near adornment.

luna: The ayah says God exalts and humbles whom He wills; it distinguishes actual divine elevation from the human assumption that reduced provision means being despised. | terra: God gives and removes dominion and gives honor and humiliation as He wills; visible authority and wealth therefore cannot decide who has truly been honored.
terra: The same address says God provides whom He wills without account, placing provision under the One who has just been named as the giver of honor and humiliation.
terra: Mary's Lord gives her a good growth, entrusts her to Zechariah, and supplies unexpected رزق; divine nurture, human guardianship, and provision meet in one child-care scene.
terra: Guardians cast their pens to decide who will care for Mary; human competition is directed toward responsibility for a dependent child.

luna: The ayah says one does not attain birr until giving from what one loves; the section’s dictionary branch for ي ت م says the orphan is neglected in his birr, and this ayah makes that goodness depend on costly giving. | terra: People do not attain birr until they spend from what they love, making release of treasured provision the test of goodness.
terra: The command to race toward forgiveness and the garden leads directly to those who spend in ease and hardship at 3:134; generous action is the field of the race.
terra: The people of taqwa spend in ease and hardship alike; the two conditions of the section become two occasions for the same generous act.

luna: The ayah says people will be tested in wealth and selves; it reinforces the section’s account of material fortune as a trial, while its own context adds injury and hardship. | terra: Believers are told they will be tested in property and persons, making ownership and loss arenas of patience rather than evidence of rank.

luna: The ayah commands that orphans receive their property and forbids replacing or consuming it; this names a concrete opposite to ikram as active care. | terra: Guardians must hand over orphan property and must not absorb it into their own; honoring the child includes preserving what is his.

luna: The ayah conditions marriage to orphan girls on fear of acting justly toward them; its own context makes fairness to a vulnerable child the test, rather than treating her as an available possession. | terra: Fear of failing justice toward orphans constrains adult household choices, making the vulnerable child's right the measure of the guardian.
terra: Within the orphan-property passage, wards not ready to manage capital must still be fed, clothed, and addressed kindly; protective delay cannot become neglect.

luna: The ayah uses the section’s root ب ل و to say to test orphans until marriageable age, then hand them their property and avoid consuming it hastily; it joins trial, childhood, delayed care, and a guardian’s duty. | terra: Guardians test orphans until maturity, then release their property without haste or exploitation; trial here serves growth into competence, not humiliation.

luna: When inheritance is divided, the ayah directs that orphans and the poor who are present receive something and kind words; it makes the orphan’s claim visible at a moment of wealth distribution. | terra: When orphans and other dependents attend an estate division, they are to receive provision and kind speech; inheritance becomes a moment of active inclusion.

luna: The ayah asks guardians to imagine leaving weak children behind in the context of orphan property; 4:10 names the consequence of consuming that property, making the orphan’s vulnerability familial. | terra: Guardians are told to imagine leaving their own weak children behind and therefore act justly; parental feeling is made the bridge to another child's protection.

luna: The ayah warns that those who consume orphan property unjustly consume fire; it marks a specific boundary opposite the section’s call to honor the orphan. | terra: Those who consume orphan property are described as eating fire, the judicial opposite of feeding and honoring the orphan.

luna: The section’s dictionary branch for ر ب ب names a wife’s son as a rabīb, and its branch for ح ج ر names the lap; this ayah joins “stepdaughters” with “in your laps” in one family ruling. | terra: ربائبكم اللاتي في حجوركم places stepdaughters and laps together, making explicit the foster-child household scene the section hears in رب and the dictionary sense of حجر.

luna: The ayah commands good treatment of orphans alongside parents, relatives, and other vulnerable neighbors; it extends the section’s family scene into social conduct. | terra: Worship of God is immediately joined to إحسان toward parents, orphans, and the needy; relation to the Lord is verified by how dependents are treated.
terra: Misers conceal what God gave from His فضل and teach others miserliness; the response to divine bounty ends in a humiliating punishment, reversing their imagined standing.

luna: The ayah addresses orphan girls whose prescribed rights are withheld; it names a concrete form of the neglect that the section’s dictionary branch of ي ت م associates with the orphan. | terra: The ruling exposes withheld entitlements of orphan women and commands justice for orphans, matching the section's sense of goodness delayed through disregard.
terra: Those who seek honor with disbelieving allies are asked whether they do not know that all honor belongs to God.

luna: The ayah says communities are tested in what they have been given and immediately tells them to race toward good works; it joins the section’s trial-by-provision image to its dictionary definition of generosity as outdoing another. | terra: God tests communities فيما آتاكم and immediately commands a race in good deeds; it joins the section's gift-as-test with its dictionary image of competing in generosity.
terra: When warning is forgotten, every gate is opened until the recipients rejoice in what they received, then seizure comes suddenly; abundance can be part of an adverse trial rather than approval.

luna: The command not to drive away those who call on God morning and evening stages a direct rejection of the socially lowly; 6:53 explains that people are tested through one another and asks whether these are the ones God favored. | terra: The Prophet must not drive away poor believers in pursuit of elite approval; vulnerable people may not be humiliated by a worldly rank calculation.

luna: This ayah uses the section’s root ب ل و for people being tested by one another, then voices the status question “Are these whom God favored?”; it directly exposes the same false reading of provision that the section corrects. | terra: God tests some people through others until the privileged ask whether these are the ones God favored; the social encounter itself exposes their false scale of honor.
terra: Those who kill their children foolishly and forbid God's provision are declared lost; child-destruction and the misreading of provision are joined in one judgment.
terra: The prohibition on killing children because of poverty is grounded in God's provision for parent and child; constriction cannot justify destroying the one needing care.

luna: The ayah forbids approaching an orphan’s property except in the best way until maturity; it protects the child’s resources while he remains too young to manage them. | terra: An orphan's property may be approached only in the best manner until maturity; absence of the father increases the guardian's duty rather than his license.

luna: The ayah uses the section’s root ب ل و for testing people through what God has given them and says they differ in rank; this separates entrusted gifts from earned standing. | terra: God raises people in differing degrees ليبلوكم في ما آتاكم; unequal gifts are examination material, not a scale of inherent honor.
terra: God replaces hardship with ease until people prosper and dismiss both as ordinary history, then takes them unawares; alternating conditions test recognition rather than reveal rank.
terra: The repeated Pharaoh-rescue scene again calls the ordeal بلاء من ربكم, relevant to the section's insistence that painful conditions remain within the Lord's trial.

luna: The section’s dictionary root ب ل و is used here for testing a people by good things and bad things, making the two-sided trial in 89:15 concrete in a historical community. | terra: Israel is tested with both good things and bad things so that they may return; this is the section's cited model for reading changing provision as تربِّي rather than rank.
terra: Victory is described as بلاء حسنا from God; the root can name a favorable testing gift, not only suffering.

luna: The ayah calls wealth and children a fitnah; this specifically connects the section’s provision and family-care images to what can test a person. | terra: Wealth and children are explicitly فتنة, turning the family prosperity heard in 89:15 into responsibility rather than certification.

luna: Orphans have a named share in the distribution of war gains; this gives the section’s call to honor them a concrete communal provision. | terra: A fixed share of communal gains is assigned to orphans and other dependents, turning honor into an institutional allocation rather than optional feeling.

luna: The command not to be impressed by a people’s wealth and children directly reverses the section’s claim that abundance proves a person honored. | terra: The Prophet is told not to admire wealth and children, for these apparent favors can become means of punishment; abundance is explicitly detached from honor.
terra: Some promise that if God gives from His فضل they will give charity and become righteous, making provision an expressly anticipated test of generosity.
terra: When God actually gives them from His فضل, they become miserly and turn away; abundance reveals the failure to pass favor onward.
terra: Their broken promise and lying leave hypocrisy in their hearts, showing that the failed prosperity-test transforms the recipient rather than certifying him.

luna: This ayah repeats the command not to be impressed by wealth and children; its repeated reversal reinforces the section’s warning against treating visible provision as rank. | terra: The warning not to admire wealth and children repeats 9:55, reinforcing that the same apparent favors can operate as punishment rather than honor.
terra: The afflicted person calls God in every posture, then after relief passes on as if he never called; restored ease fails to produce remembered dependence.
terra: When people taste mercy after adversity, they scheme against God's signs; the favorable turn is received as license rather than accountable care.
terra: The Prophet is consoled that all honor belongs to God, setting a firm boundary against human assignment of worth.
terra: When mercy is removed after being tasted, the human becomes despairing and ungrateful; constriction is immediately misread just as in ربي أهانن.
terra: When favor follows hardship, the human turns exultant and boastful; expansion is misread just as in ربي أكرمن.
terra: The patient people who do good are the stated exception to the despair and boastfulness of 11:9-10, showing the fitting response across both conditions.
terra: Noah's elite dismiss his followers as the lowest people and judge them by superficial opinion, illustrating human rank inferred from visible condition.
terra: Noah refuses to drive believers away and says their account is with their Lord; elite preference cannot dictate who receives the messenger's care.
terra: Noah will not say that God grants no good to those whom elite eyes despise; visible poverty cannot establish divine humiliation.
terra: Abraham promptly brings a roasted calf to the messengers who arrive with good news, another concrete Quranic scene in which receiving guests means feeding them.

luna: The Egyptian asks his wife to honor Joseph’s lodging and considers taking him as a son; this makes the section’s foster-child sense of ر ب ب and its account of ك ر م as an act toward another concrete. | terra: أكرمي مثواه is an instruction to honor the displaced child Joseph in the household, with the hope of taking him as a son; ikram is enacted care, not a status he boasts of.
terra: When Joseph reaches maturity God gives him judgment and knowledge; it completes the child-in-household scene of 12:21 with growth into adulthood.

luna: The ayah says people rejoice in worldly life while its enjoyment is only brief, alongside God’s extending and restricting provision with the section’s root ق د ر; it loosens the link between a large share and lasting honor. | terra: God expands provision and measures it narrowly, while people rejoice in the nearer life; the verse separates fluctuating رزق from enduring value.
terra: Moses recalls rescue from Pharaoh's torment as containing a great trial from the Lord, tying remembered affliction to gratitude for deliverance.
terra: Increase is tied to gratitude and severe consequence to ingratitude; the decisive issue in received favor is response, not possession.
terra: Lot identifies the visitors as his guests and asks his people not to disgrace him through their treatment, making a host responsible for another's protected standing.
terra: The command not to shame the guests places honor at the boundary between sheltering a vulnerable visitor and exposing him to abuse.
terra: Every نعمة is said to come from God, and distress makes people cry to Him; it fixes the source of both the remembered ease and the appeal under restriction.
terra: When distress is removed, some immediately associate others with their Lord, showing relief failing to mature into grateful recognition.
terra: Their response is described as ingratitude for what God gave, making enjoyment a temporarily permitted test with consequences.
terra: A father receives news of a daughter with a darkened face, treating the arrival of a dependent child as damage to his own standing.
terra: He considers keeping her على هون or burying her, the stark reversal of taking a vulnerable child into a nurturing embrace.
terra: Unequal provision is used to expose denial of God's نعمة, preventing the larger share from becoming an independent personal entitlement.
terra: Spouses, children, grandchildren, and good provision are named together as divine gifts, followed by the charge that people deny God's favor.
terra: People recognize God's نعمة and then deny it, precisely the failure of memory that lets received care stop at the self.
terra: A secure town receiving abundant provision from every place becomes ungrateful for God's favors and is made to taste hunger and fear; plenty and restriction form one moral trial.
terra: The well-provided town also receives a messenger from among itself and rejects him; its later deprivation follows failed response to both provision and guidance.
terra: After the town's reversal, recipients are commanded to eat God's lawful good provision and be grateful for His favor; gratitude is the proper reading of supply.
terra: God extends عطآء ربك to both seekers of this world and seekers of the next; receiving from the Lord is universal examination material rather than exclusive approval.
terra: Worldly differences in فضل are visible, but the next life's degrees are greater; the verse prevents present provision from becoming the final hierarchy.

luna: This neighboring command tells children to show kindness to parents in old age; 17:24 supplies the reason in its own contribution, remembering how they raised the child when small. | terra: The grown child must treat aged parents with إحسان and قولاً كريماً; the care once received returns as concrete honorable treatment.

luna: The section’s dictionary branch for ر ب ب describes raising someone through stages; the adult’s prayer remembers that his parents raised him صغيرًا and asks God to show them mercy in return. | terra: The prayer كما ربياني صغيرا explicitly recalls parents raising the speaker when small and asks the Lord to repay that nurture with mercy.

luna: The ayah commands giving the orphan his due; it turns the section’s shift from claiming one’s own honor to performing an obligation for someone else into a material act. | terra: Kin, the poor, and the traveler are assigned a due before the passage names the Lord's expansion and restriction of provision at 17:30.
terra: Even when one must turn away while awaiting provision, one must speak gently to the claimant; lack of means does not authorize humiliation.
terra: The hand must be neither chained to the neck nor opened without limit; it locates honorable giving between miserliness and self-ruining excess before 17:30 names variable provision.

luna: The ayah says God extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it; it uses the section’s root ق د ر for this change, rather than validating the claim “my Lord has humiliated me.” | terra: The Lord both expands رزق and restricts it, placing the giving duties of 17:26-29 under divine apportionment rather than a verdict on worth.

luna: The ayah forbids killing children for fear of poverty and says God provides for both parent and child; it makes scarcity a boundary against withholding care from a child. | terra: Fear of poverty must not lead to killing children, because God provides for them and their parents; expected restriction is no warrant for withheld life and care.

luna: The ayah repeats the duty to guard an orphan’s property in the best manner until maturity; it makes sustained protection, rather than possession by the guardian, the measure of care. | terra: The orphan's property is protected until maturity and the covenant must be fulfilled; care continues over time when the child lacks a father's defense.
terra: God honors all children of Adam and provides them with good things; human dignity precedes differing shares of wealth and cannot be inferred from their size.
terra: Favor makes the human turn away arrogantly, while harm makes him despair, compressing the section's two mistaken readings into one verse.

luna: The ayah uses the section’s root ب ل و for testing who does best in deeds through the earth’s adornment; it shifts attention from possessing comfort to what a person does with it. | terra: Earth's adornment is made a test of who acts best, directly classifying attractive worldly possession as examination material.

luna: The command to remain with those who call on God and not turn one’s gaze away toward worldly adornment draws a specific boundary against preferring visible status over humble people. | terra: The Prophet must remain with devoted poor believers and not look past them toward worldly adornment, reversing attention based on visible provision.
terra: The garden owner says he has more wealth and a stronger following, explicitly converting provision into a claim of superior rank.
terra: The wealthy man enters his garden while wronging himself and declares that it will never perish, turning a received estate into imagined permanence.
terra: He doubts the Hour and assumes that even a return to his Lord would yield something better, carrying worldly advantage into a claim of divine rank.
terra: His companion says the sight of the garden should have prompted recognition that power belongs to God, even when the speaker has fewer goods and children.
terra: His produce is destroyed and he wrings his hands over what he spent, collapsing the status claim of 18:34 and exposing wealth's contingency.
terra: When loss comes, no social group can help the garden owner against God and he cannot help himself; the following and wealth once used as rank prove powerless.
terra: The garden scene closes by assigning true protection to God and calling His reward and outcome better, replacing the owner's material scale.

luna: The ayah calls wealth and children worldly adornment but says lasting good deeds are better; it sets the section’s perceived signs of honor against durable conduct. | terra: Wealth and children are the adornment of the nearer life, while lasting good deeds are better with the Lord; possession and enduring worth are placed on different scales.

luna: Moses and his companion preserve treasure for two orphan boys until they grow up; this is a particular scene of a child’s future being protected when his father is absent. | terra: A wall preserves a righteous father's treasure for two orphan boys until maturity; providential delay protects their good, reversing the neglectful delay named in the section's dictionary note.
terra: Disbelievers point to the two parties' comparative station and assembly, using visible social setting as an argument against revelation.
terra: God recalls generations with better furnishings and appearance whom He destroyed, refuting the claim that impressive worldly station signals worth.
terra: The Merciful may extend the straying person's condition until the promised consequence reveals who truly has the worse station and weaker support.
terra: A disbeliever confidently claims that he will be given wealth and children, converting hoped-for provision into proof of continuing privilege.
terra: God will inherit what the claimant speaks of and he will come alone, stripping wealth and children from the status claim.
terra: The infant Moses is placed under God's bestowed love and fashioned تحت عيني; divine care operates through a precarious foster setting before the child can protect himself.

luna: Moses recounts being returned to his mother so she could be comforted and not grieve; this repeated account joins the section’s image of nurture to the relief of a parent. | terra: Moses is returned to his mother, passes through repeated trials فتونا, and arrives at a measured time; nurturing and testing unfold as one long process.
terra: Moses defines the Lord as the One who gives each thing its form and then guides it, a divine answer to Pharaoh's claim of having raised him.

luna: The command not to fix one’s gaze on others’ worldly adornment says it is a test; this directly checks the section’s human inference that visible ease proves divine honor. | terra: Worldly splendor is something God uses to test groups, while رزق ربك is better and more lasting; visible luxury therefore cannot be the section's imagined rank.

luna: The section’s dictionary form of ب ل و means testing; this ayah explicitly says both harm and good are a fitnah, so abundance and constriction can each be a trial rather than a rank. | terra: The section's two-sided definition of divine testing is stated exactly here: God tests with both harm and good, so neither condition by itself is a verdict of honor.
terra: Human development is traced through successive embryonic states, childhood, and maturity, a bodily instance of the section's dictionary definition of gradual nurture to completion.

luna: The section cites the wording that whoever God humiliates has no one to honor him; this sets true divine judgment apart from a person merely inferring humiliation from scarcity. | terra: ومن يهن الله فما له من مكرم gives the true boundary of humiliation and honor: neither abundant nor restricted رزق lets a human assign God's verdict.
terra: Successive transformations culminate in another creation, giving concrete form to development حالا فحالا even though the رب root is not used in the ayah.

luna: This ayah specifies the wealth and children being extended; 23:56 supplies the question whether these mean good is being hastened, making the gifts themselves the section’s test rather than proof of honor. | terra: The question names wealth and sons as what God keeps extending to some people, exactly the family abundance the human of the section mistakes for approval.

luna: This continuation answers the question in 23:55: those gifts are not proof that good is being hastened to their owners, completing the section’s reversal of wealth as rank. | terra: The answer rejects the inference that extended wealth and sons mean God is hastening good for them; this is a direct correction of ربي أكرمن.
terra: Those who give remain fearful because they will return to their Lord; giving is not converted into a boast of assured rank.
terra: These givers race in good deeds and reach them first, closely realizing the section's dictionary picture of a contest in generosity.
terra: People of فضل and ample means are forbidden to stop supporting relatives and the poor after an injury; possessed favor must become pardoning, continued favor.

luna: The ayah says some people are made a trial for others and asks whether they will be patient; it makes the section’s meeting of the well-provided person and the vulnerable orphan a test of how people treat each other. | terra: God makes some people a trial for others and asks whether they will be patient; differing human conditions test both the needy and those able to respond.
terra: The servants of the Merciful spend neither extravagantly nor stingily, giving a measured form to responsible use of provision.

luna: Pharaoh asks Moses whether he was not raised among them as a child; the section cites this use of ر ب ب to show human upbringing being invoked as a claim over the grown child. | terra: Pharaoh claims ألم نربك فينا وليدا, invoking household upbringing as a debt; it supplies the section's child-raised-under-authority scene while questioning ownership of that care.
luna: Pharaoh’s next line accuses Moses of a past deed after claiming to have raised him in 26:18; this shows how care can be wielded as leverage by a powerful guardian.
terra: Moses answers Pharaoh's claimed upbringing by pointing to Pharaoh's enslavement of Israel; care used as leverage is exposed as a compromised نعمة.
terra: Abraham identifies his Lord as the One who created and guides him, beginning a sequence of sustaining acts that makes رب active care.
terra: The Lord is the One who feeds and gives drink, placing provision within ongoing nurture rather than social honor.
terra: Healing when ill extends Lordly care beyond abundance into bodily adversity.
terra: Death and restored life complete Abraham's account of the Lord's governance through changing human states.
terra: Noah's people object that the lowest people follow him, making social inferiority their reason to reject truth.
terra: Noah refuses to expel the believers, preserving vulnerable followers against the powerful audience's status demand.
terra: Solomon calls an extraordinary gift فضل ربي ليبلوني and asks whether he will be grateful; abundance is consciously received as a test rather than proof of personal worth.

luna: God tells Moses’ mother to nurse him and, when afraid, place him in the river without fear; the infant-care scene makes the section’s picture of a child nourished and protected tangible. | terra: Moses' mother is told to nurse him and promised his return before exposing him to the river, joining maternal care, fear, and divine guardianship.
terra: Pharaoh's wife protects the found infant and proposes taking him as a son, a direct household reversal from exposed child to cherished child.

luna: This ayah continues 28:7 by having Moses’ sister watch the infant from a distance after he is placed in the river; it contributes the family’s protective follow-up. | terra: Moses' mother sends his sister to follow him from a distance, adding vigilant family concern to the exposed infant's foster-care scene.

luna: After 28:11’s watch, Moses’ sister offers to direct the household to someone who will care for him when he refuses other nurses; it continues the infant-care scene. | terra: After Moses refuses other wet nurses, his sister directs the household to a family that will nurture him sincerely; provision, nursing, and restored kinship converge.

luna: The ayah says Moses was returned to his mother so she would be comforted and not grieve; it completes the caregiving scene of 28:7 and gives reunion its own contribution. | terra: God restores Moses to his mother so her eye may be comforted and she may not grieve; the child's shelter is shown as divine care delivered through restored family embrace.
terra: Qarun's vast stores lead to exultation, beginning the Quran's fullest scene of abundance being mistaken for personal distinction.
terra: Qarun is told to seek the next life, do good as God did good to him, and avoid corruption; received favor is expressly redirected into outward good.

luna: Qarun says he was given his wealth because of knowledge he possessed; this is the same self-attribution of abundance that the section sets against God’s will in 28:82. | terra: Qarun says he received wealth because of knowledge he possesses, the same self-attribution corrected as فتنة in 39:49.
terra: Those desiring worldly life wish for Qarun's share when he appears in splendor, displaying the spectators' false equation of wealth with honor.
terra: People of knowledge answer that God's reward is better for faith and good work, supplying the correct scale before Qarun's fall.
terra: The earth swallows Qarun and no faction can help him, physically erasing the social height inferred from his provision.

luna: After Qarun is swallowed by the earth, those who had wanted his place recognize that God expands provision for whom He wills and restricts it; this gives the section’s correction a scene of repentant witnesses. | terra: After Qarun is swallowed up, yesterday's admirers finally say that God expands provision and restricts it; the collapse corrects their reading of wealth as honor.

luna: The ayah repeats that God expands provision for whom He wills and restricts it, using the section’s root ق د ر and reinforcing that variation in provision does not itself rank its recipient. | terra: God expands provision for whom He wills and measures it narrowly; the repeated formula directly matches فَقَدَرَ عَلَيْهِ رِزْقَهُ without calling the latter disgrace.
terra: People rejoice when made to taste mercy and despair when harm follows their own deeds; the emotional swing parallels the two hasty verdicts in the section.

luna: The ayah asks people to notice that God expands provision for whom He wills and restricts it with the section’s root ق د ر; this directly counters judging honor by material ease. | terra: The alternation between expanded and restricted provision is offered as a sign, not a ranking of the recipients.
terra: Immediately after the provision formula, the recipient is told to give kin, poor, and traveler their due; provision is read by what one does with it.

luna: The ayah recalls a mother carrying her child through weakness and nursing him for two years, then commands gratitude to parents; it supplies the bodily care behind the section’s family image. | terra: A mother's weakness upon weakness and two years of weaning make parental nurture concrete, and gratitude to God is paired with gratitude to the parents who carried it.
terra: Adopted sons are not made biological sons merely by declaration, supplying a legal boundary around household care and claimed parenthood.
terra: Adopted children should be called by their fathers when known and otherwise treated as brothers and clients, preserving belonging without falsifying lineage.
terra: Saba is told to eat from its Lord's provision and be grateful amid two flourishing gardens; an ample land is explicitly a scene of accountable favor.
terra: When the people turn away, the flood replaces their productive gardens with bitter growth, reversing abundance without changing the identity of the Lord.
terra: The reversal is identified as recompense for ingratitude, locating the judgment in response to favor rather than in the mere possession or loss of it.

luna: The affluent claim that greater wealth and children mean they will not be punished; their boast is a direct instance of reading provision as honor, which the section challenges. | terra: The affluent claim that greater wealth and children mean they will not be punished, directly voicing the inference rejected in the section.

luna: The ayah answers the boast in 34:35 by saying God expands provision for whom He wills and restricts it with the section’s root ق د ر; distribution, not human status, controls the scene. | terra: The Prophet is told to answer affluent deniers that his Lord expands provision and restricts it; their abundance does not validate their claim of immunity.

luna: The ayah completes 34:35 and 34:36 by saying wealth and children do not bring people near to God; it draws the boundary between worldly means and actual standing. | terra: Wealth and children do not bring anyone near to God; faith and good action do, replacing possession with accountable conduct as the measure.
terra: The same expansion-and-restriction formula is joined to God's replacement of whatever one spends, making generosity the response to provision in either measure.
terra: Whoever seeks honor is told that all honor belongs to God and that good words and deeds rise, redirecting status from possessions to accountable action.
terra: The slain believer wishes his people knew that his Lord forgave him and made him among the honored, locating genuine ikram beyond worldly standing.
terra: The people of the garden receive fruits and are مكرمون; it is a true divine honor after judgment, unlike the provisional نعمة misread in the section.

luna: This ayah stages Abraham’s command to his son and the son’s response; 37:106 names the scene a clear trial, connecting the section’s test image to family attachment without confusing it with prosperity. | terra: When Abraham's son reaches the age of working beside him, father and child face the dream together; a nurtured child becomes the center of a grave test, not a possession proving favor.

luna: This ayah names the father-and-son scene in 37:102 a clear trial, making explicit that a family bond, too, can be the setting of ibtilāʾ. | terra: God explicitly calls the father-son ordeal the clear trial, bringing family love and divine testing into the same scene.
terra: The son is ransomed with a great sacrifice, so the trial ends in preserved life rather than treating the child as expendable property.
terra: In adversity the human calls his Lord, but after نعمة he forgets the earlier dependence; changing conditions expose a failed memory of care.

luna: The section cites this correction to a person who attributes a gift to his own knowledge: the ayah calls the granted blessing a fitnah, directly reversing the reading of provision as proof of merit. | terra: After relief, the person claims the favor came through personal knowledge; بَلْ هِيَ فِتْنَةٌ gives the same correction as the section: the gift is a test.
terra: Earlier peoples made the same self-attributing claim as the person in 39:49, and what they earned did not avail them.
terra: The consequences of those people's deeds struck them, and the present wrongdoers are warned likewise; the gift-as-entitlement claim has a concrete end.

luna: The ayah asks whether people know God expands and restricts provision at will, using the section’s root ق د ر; it supports the distinction between divine distribution and the human verdict of being honored or despised. | terra: After the claimant's wealth fails him, the passage asks whether people know that God expands and restricts provision; this supplies the lesson of 39:49 in explicit terms.
terra: Creation proceeds from dust and embryo to child, maturity, and old age; the measured stages illuminate the section's account of Lordly upbringing.
terra: The human never tires of asking for good but despairs when harm touches him, revealing attachment to condition rather than trust in the Giver.
terra: Mercy after adversity prompts the claim هذا لي and imagined entitlement in the next life; granted relief is converted into personal rank.
terra: Favor makes the human withdraw, while evil brings prolonged prayer; it completes the unstable relation to good and harm described at 41:49-50.

luna: The ayah says God expands or restricts provision for whom He wills and places the keys of heaven and earth under His authority; it repeats the section’s root ق د ر while grounding provision in divine rule. | terra: Ownership of the heavens' and earth's stores accompanies the statement that God expands and restricts رزق; the determining authority is the Provider, not social standing.

luna: The ayah says provision would lead people to transgress if expanded without limit, so God sends it down by measure; the section’s dictionary root ق د ر names this limit as measured provision rather than contempt. | terra: The verse explains that unrestricted abundance could make servants transgress, so God sends provision in a measure; restriction can itself be calibrated care.
terra: Mercy makes people rejoice and consequences make them ungrateful; the verse supplies another explicit reversal between reception and interpretation.
terra: Daughters and sons alike are described as gifts God grants as He wills, correcting the parent who treats a daughter as humiliation.
terra: God combines sons and daughters or leaves whom He wills childless, placing every family configuration under gift and measure rather than social rank.
terra: God says worldly unbelief could have been accompanied by houses with silver roofs, showing that luxury is too indiscriminate to certify honor.
terra: Silver stairways, doors, and couches continue the deliberately extravagant counterexample begun at 43:33.
terra: Gold adornment is declared merely the enjoyment of worldly life, while the next life belongs with the Lord to the people of taqwa.
terra: Pharaoh calls Moses مهين while boasting of his own kingdom and bracelets; it exemplifies humiliation issued by a contemptuous ruler on the basis of visible status.

luna: In Hell the boastful offender is taunted as “mighty, noble”; the ironic use of ك ر ي م reverses the section’s question of what genuine honor means. | terra: The condemned person is told mockingly that he is العزيز الكريم; the irony strips worldly self-importance of any claim to genuine karam.

luna: The ayah remembers a mother’s hardship in carrying and bearing a child and marks his growth to maturity; it makes the section’s child-reared-through-stages image explicit. | terra: Pregnancy, birth, nursing, and mature gratitude form a full arc from received care to the adult's prayer for parents and descendants.
terra: Those called to spend may be stingy, but their stinginess is against themselves while God is rich and they are poor; dependence cannot be hidden by possession.

luna: The section cites the ayah’s use of أكرمكم: the most honored before God is the most God-conscious, not the person with the most provision. | terra: أكرمكم عند الله أتقاكم supplies the measure the section says the prosperous person gets wrong: honor before God rests on taqwa, not abundance.
terra: Abraham's visitors are called ضيف إبراهيم المكرمين, introducing an honored-guest scene in which honor is immediately enacted as feeding.
terra: Abraham quietly goes to his household and brings a fat calf, supplying the costly deed behind the guests' description as honored.
terra: He brings the food near and invites them to eat; ikram is proximity, provision, and service offered to another.
terra: Believers must spend from what God made them successors over, recasting ownership as temporary stewardship.

luna: The ayah distinguishes those who spent before victory from those who spent later while promising good to both; it gives a concrete Quranic scene for the section’s dictionary image of outdoing another in generosity. | terra: Those who spend before victory receive a higher degree than later spenders; Quranic rank is attached to timely generosity, not simply to having resources.
terra: Charitable men and women who make a good loan receive multiplication and أجر كريم; noble reward is attached to outward generosity.

luna: The ayah names mutual boasting and competition in increasing wealth and children as features of worldly life; this directly parallels the section’s mistaken use of abundance as rank. | terra: Worldly life is portrayed as adornment and rivalry in wealth and children that flourishes and then withers; the scene makes prosperous status visibly temporary.
terra: Those who are miserly and command miserliness are reminded that God is self-sufficient; retained wealth supplies no independence from Him.
terra: God raises believers and people of knowledge in degrees, locating genuine elevation in faith and knowledge rather than possessions.

luna: The ayah assigns a share of communal wealth to orphans and other vulnerable groups so wealth will not circulate only among the rich; it directly counters using abundance as a private rank. | terra: Orphans receive a designated share so that wealth does not circulate only among the rich; the verse directly overturns possession as social honor.
terra: The Helpers prefer others even while having privation themselves, showing that restricted means can disclose honor through generosity.
terra: The hypocrites plan to stop spending so the Prophet's companions will disperse, using control of provision as an instrument of abasement.
terra: Their boast that the mightier will expel the lowlier is reversed by the declaration that true might belongs to God, His Messenger, and the believers.

luna: Like the section’s account of blessing as a trial, this ayah names wealth and children themselves as a fitnah, making care and resources responsibilities as well as gifts. | terra: The repeated declaration that wealth and children are only a trial directly corrects the human reading of being enriched and indulged as honor.
terra: The command to spend is paired with deliverance from one's own greed; the decisive test of provision occurs in the act of releasing it.
terra: A good loan to God is multiplied and forgiven, presenting released wealth as the route through which provision yields good.
terra: Housing, pregnancy support, and payment for nursing require continued care even after separation; it supplies the family obligation that 65:7 scales to the giver's means.

luna: For a person whose provision is restricted, the ayah commands spending from what God has given; it repeats the section’s wording from the root ق د ر and connects constriction with care measured to one’s means. | terra: The person whose provision is restricted must still spend from what God gave him; constriction is neither humiliation nor release from caring for another.
terra: The garden owners are tested through a productive estate, joining the section's prosperous trial to a scene in which the recipients soon fail the needy.
terra: A visitation from the Lord circles the garden while its owners sleep, showing that the estate used to exclude the poor remains wholly exposed to divine action.
terra: The garden becomes like a harvested field before the owners arrive; the object of their proprietary certainty is removed in a night.
terra: The owners resolve that no poor person shall enter the garden that day; this is the concrete withholding exposed by the prosperity-test begun at 68:17.
terra: The most balanced owner recalls having urged them to glorify God, identifying forgotten Lordship inside the failed garden test.
terra: The owners finally glorify their Lord and confess wrongdoing, replacing possessive certainty with accountable recognition.
terra: After the garden's loss, its owners hope their Lord will replace it with better and turn their desire toward Him; failed provision becomes a chance to return.
terra: Failure to urge the feeding of the poor is named among the causes of punishment, closely repeating the social omission next to the orphan in the section's surah.
terra: The human is introduced as anxiously constituted before 70:20-21 show panic under harm and withholding under good; it names the disposition behind both readings.
terra: When harm touches the ordinary human being he panics; it is one half of the unstable response to changing conditions that the section diagnoses.
terra: When good touches him he withholds, directly connecting prosperity to the failure to pass care onward.
terra: The exception is those whose wealth contains a recognized right, making ownership carry an obligation rather than a rank.
terra: That recognized right belongs to the petitioner and the deprived, the very people whom self-reading prosperity tends to overlook.
terra: The people who reserve that share are finally في جنات مكرمون; real honor follows faithful obligations rather than merely receiving wealth.
terra: وقد خلقكم أطوارا states that God created people in stages, a concise nonlexical parallel to the cited definition of رب as bringing a thing through states.
terra: Abundant water is promised in the hypothetical scene of steadfastness; 72:17 then identifies that very abundance as the medium of a test.
terra: لنفتنهم فيه makes the plentiful water of 72:16 a trial within provision, directly blocking the inference that ample supply equals divine rank.
terra: The condemned admit that they did not feed the poor, making withheld nourishment a disclosed reason for their final abasement.
terra: People love the immediate life, naming the preference that turns present provision into the dominant scale.
terra: They leave the hereafter behind, identifying what the near-life preference excludes from their judgment.
terra: The human is created from a mixed drop in order to be tested and is equipped with hearing and sight; nurture and trial begin together at human origin.

luna: The righteous feed the orphan, the poor, and the captive despite loving the food themselves; this is a direct act of generous care rather than a claim to status. | terra: The righteous feed an orphan and other helpless people with food they themselves love; ikram appears as costly action directed outward.

luna: After 76:8 depicts feeding the orphan, poor, and captive, this ayah says the feeders seek no repayment or thanks; it makes care an act toward the vulnerable rather than a claim to honor. | terra: The feeders seek neither repayment nor thanks, distinguishing care of the vulnerable from a generosity contest performed for personal rank.

luna: The ayah opens with turning away; 80:2 identifies the arriving blind man, making this a specific scene of the neglect the section’s dictionary note associates with the orphan. | terra: The Prophet frowns and turns away, beginning a correction of attention distributed by perceived social standing.

luna: This ayah identifies the blind man who came in the scene begun by 80:1; it gives a concrete vulnerable petitioner whose arrival is met with neglect. | terra: The person from whom he turns is blind and has actively come for guidance, marking the overlooked party as vulnerable yet seeking benefit.

luna: This ayah introduces the person who considers himself self-sufficient; 80:6 shows attention being directed to him, a specific social-status contrast to neglecting the orphan. | terra: The self-sufficient man receives the privileged attention, echoing the false rank attached to perceived independence.

luna: This ayah shows the speaker devoting attention to the self-sufficient man introduced in 80:5; 80:8 and 80:10 describe attention diverted from the striver, exposing status-based regard. | terra: The Prophet attends closely to that self-sufficient person, making status-based allocation of care visible as an action.

luna: This ayah introduces the person who comes striving; 80:10 says attention is diverted from him, a concrete parallel to the section’s neglected orphan. | terra: The other man comes striving, supplying the moral quality hidden by his low social visibility.
luna: This ayah says the striver of 80:8 comes in fear of God; 80:10 then describes turning away from him, sharpening the contrast between moral worth and received attention.

luna: This ayah says attention is diverted from the striving petitioner introduced in 80:8; it completes the scene of overlooking the vulnerable while attending to the self-sufficient man in 80:5 and 80:6. | terra: The striving, fearful man is neglected, a direct social reversal of honoring the person most in need of reception.
terra: The buried girl is brought forward as the questioned party, restoring voice and standing to the child whose family erased her.
terra: The question asks for what sin she was killed, exposing the absolute injustice of turning a dependent child's existence into family disgrace.
terra: ما غرك بربك الكريم addresses a person deceived about his generous Lord; it tightly links رب and كريم while exposing the same misuse of divine generosity.
terra: The generous Lord of 82:6 is the One who created, proportioned, and balanced the person, making His generosity formative care rather than material indulgence alone.
terra: God composes the human in whatever form He wills, completing the picture of measured Lordly formation.
terra: People prefer the worldly life, a concise diagnosis of why its expansion can be mistaken for honor.
terra: The hereafter is better and more lasting, supplying the scale omitted by that preference.
terra: The person has not attempted the steep path, introducing care for the captive, orphan, and destitute as the difficult use of human capacity.
terra: The question asks what can make the steep path known, marking the following acts as the demanding measure of worth.
terra: Freeing a person from bondage begins the path, placing social release beside feeding an orphan under scarcity.

luna: This ayah names feeding during severe hunger; 90:15 specifies an orphan of near kin, so the cited detail places material care inside the section’s family image. | terra: Feeding is located on a day of severe hunger, so constrained conditions become the setting for generosity rather than an excuse to withhold it.

luna: This ayah identifies a near-relative orphan; 90:14 supplies feeding during severe hunger, joining kinship and orphanhood in the section’s family-care scene. | terra: The recipient in that famine scene is an orphan of near kin, joining lost family protection to concrete food and renewed kinship.

luna: This ayah identifies the poor person in the same feeding passage as 90:14 and 90:15; it extends that passage’s concrete care from the near-relative orphan to a destitute person. | terra: The famine feeding also reaches a destitute person in the dust, widening outward care beyond the related orphan of 90:15.
terra: The generous person who gives and practices taqwa begins the path of ease, joining giving to the very criterion of honor in 49:13.
terra: The giver affirms the best promise, distinguishing his inward reading of provision from the miser's denial.
terra: God eases the giver toward ease, continuing the outcome attached to generosity rather than hoarded abundance.
terra: The opposite person is miserly and deems himself self-sufficient; perceived independence turns received abundance into withheld care.
terra: The self-sufficient miser denies the best promise, stating the inner counterpart of his withholding.
terra: He is eased toward hardship, reversing his assumption that retained wealth secures ease.
terra: His wealth cannot avail when he falls, exposing the false security on which the miser's self-ranking rested.
terra: The أتقى person is kept from the fire, linking the Quran's highest piety term to the giver described in the next verse.
terra: He gives his wealth to purify himself; the possession becomes a means of moral growth only when passed onward.
terra: The giver will finally be satisfied by his Lord, closing the passage in which taqwa and spending, rather than wealth retained, establish his standing.

luna: The ayah recalls that God found the Prophet an orphan and gave him shelter; the section’s principle that one who was sheltered should shelter others is grounded in this personal history. | terra: God finds the Prophet an orphan and gives shelter; this is the section's decisive pattern of the child without a father receiving a new protective embrace.

luna: This neighboring grace recalls the Prophet’s need and God’s provision for him; beside the orphan-shelter memory in 93:6 and the command in 93:9, it links received care to later responsibility. | terra: God finds the Prophet in need and enriches him, setting received provision immediately before duties toward the orphan and petitioner.

luna: The ayah directly commands that the orphan not be oppressed; after the Prophet’s own shelter in 93:6, it turns care received into care owed. | terra: Because the addressee was sheltered as an orphan, he is commanded not to overpower the orphan; received care must become care.

luna: Following the command not to oppress the orphan in 93:9, this ayah says not to rebuff the asker; it extends the section’s care ethic to another vulnerable petitioner. | terra: The petitioner must not be rebuffed, extending the anti-humiliation command from the orphan to another dependent person at the door.
terra: The Lord's نعمة is to be voiced after the commands concerning orphan and petitioner; blessing is acknowledged through responsible remembrance, not private rank.
terra: Ease is promised with hardship, discouraging the restricted person from reading difficulty as abandonment.
terra: The repeated promise that ease accompanies hardship reinforces that constriction is not a final verdict of humiliation.
terra: وربك الأكرم names the Lord as most generous before 96:6-7 expose the human who sees himself self-sufficient; the sequence contrasts source and recipient.
terra: The human transgresses precisely at the point where divine creation and generosity should have produced gratitude.
terra: أن رآه استغنى identifies seeing oneself as self-sufficient as the cause of transgression, the inner error behind hoarding divine care.
terra: The human is intensely ungrateful to his Lord, supplying the moral diagnosis behind receiving nurture yet failing the dependent.
terra: His intense love of wealth gives that ingratitude a material object and helps explain why received provision stops with him.
terra: Rivalry in abundance distracts people, directly portraying possessions and numbers as a competition for rank.
terra: The distraction lasts until the graves, giving the abundance-rivalry its terminal boundary before questioning about نعيم.
terra: People will be questioned about النعيم, turning enjoyed ease from a badge of honor into an accountable trust.
terra: The slanderer amasses wealth and repeatedly counts it, a concrete scene of possession becoming self-absorption rather than care.
terra: He imagines his wealth has made him permanent, an extreme form of treating provision as a durable personal rank.
terra: Denial of judgment introduces the repulsion of the orphan at 107:2, rooting failed care in a false account of responsibility.

luna: The ayah says the denier pushes the orphan away; this gives a concrete scene for the section’s dictionary explanation that the orphan is neglected. | terra: The denier violently repels the orphan, the clearest opposite of honoring and gathering the fatherless child into care.

luna: This ayah after 107:2 says he does not urge feeding the poor; it continues the rebuke from rejecting the orphan to withholding encouragement for material care. | terra: Failure even to urge feeding the poor accompanies repelling the orphan, showing neglect as a social habit rather than a lack of private sentiment.
terra: The passage ends with people withholding even small ordinary assistance, extending orphan-neglect into a settled habit of stopping benefit.
